indicators.label: A/D Line
indicators.theory: The advance/decline line is the best-known breadth indicator and the simplest to compute: each day, take the number of stocks that rose, subtract the number that fell, and add the result to the previous day's value. Every stock counts the same, whatever its size.
indicators.interpretation: Because it isn't cap-weighted, the A/D line shows whether a move is broad or carried by a few giants. Watch for divergences: if the index makes new highs while the A/D line falls, most stocks are no longer participating and the advance is fragile. It is a warning, not a timing signal: divergences can last for months.

indicators.label: Net Advances (ADn)
indicators.theory: Daily advances minus declines, ratio-adjusted: (advances − declines) ÷ (advances + declines) × 1,000. Normalizing by the number of stocks traded makes readings comparable over time and across markets. It is the raw input to the McClellan Oscillator and the Summation Index.
indicators.interpretation: Each bar is one day's breadth. Readings above +800 or below −800 mean nearly every stock moved the same way (a thrust day). Strings of positive bars confirm a healthy rally; heavy negative days clustered together often mark capitulation near lows.

indicators.label: Summation Index & RASI
indicators.theory: The McClellan Summation Index is the running total of the McClellan Oscillator. The ratio-adjusted version (RASI) uses the ratio-adjusted oscillator, so it doesn't depend on how many stocks are counted. Both turn short-term breadth swings into a medium-term trend.
indicators.interpretation: Rising = breadth is improving, falling = deteriorating; the direction matters more than the level. On RASI, crossing above 0 is a bullish sign, above +500 the market is overbought (often a sign of strong momentum early in a rally), and below −500 it is oversold, where major lows tend to form.

indicators.label: McClellan Oscillator
indicators.theory: The difference between a 19-day and a 39-day exponential average (10% and 5% smoothing) of ratio-adjusted net advances. It measures the short-term momentum of breadth, much like MACD does for prices.
indicators.interpretation: Above zero, advancing stocks dominate; below zero, decliners do. Readings above +70 are overbought and below −70 oversold; beyond ±100 they are extreme. Zero crossings and divergences against the index (e.g. a new index low with a higher oscillator low) are the classic signals.

indicators.label: New Highs & Lows
indicators.theory: The number of stocks hitting a new 52-week high (green, up) and a new 52-week low (red, down) each day, based on intraday highs and lows. The line is the net (highs − lows), averaged over 10 days.
indicators.interpretation: In a healthy uptrend new highs clearly outnumber new lows. Rising new lows while the index is near its highs is a sign of internal weakness. A spike in new lows usually comes with sell-offs, and its fading tends to signal that the selling is exhausted.

indicators.label: % Above Moving Averages
indicators.theory: The percentage of stocks closing above their own 20-day (short term), 50-day (medium term) and 200-day (long term) moving averages.
indicators.interpretation: Above 50% the majority of stocks are in an uptrend for that time frame. Readings above 80% are overbought and below 20% oversold, especially on the 20- and 50-day lines. When the index rises while these percentages fall, fewer stocks are carrying the move. The 200-day line describes the long-term health of the market.

indicators.label: % at Highs vs Lows
indicators.theory: The High-Low Index: new 52-week highs as a percentage of new highs plus new lows, NH ÷ (NH + NL) × 100, averaged over 10 days. Days with no new highs or lows don't change the average.
indicators.interpretation: Above 50% more stocks are making new highs than new lows; below 50%, the reverse. Above 70% indicates a strong uptrend, below 30% a strong downtrend. A move from below 30% to above 50% often confirms that a correction has ended.

indicators.label: Volume
indicators.theory: The share of total volume traded in advancing stocks: up volume ÷ (up volume + down volume) × 100. It weighs breadth by how much money is moving, not just by how many stocks.
indicators.interpretation: Days above 90% (90% up days) show heavy, broad buying; days below 10% (90% down days) show panic selling. Clusters of 90% down days often precede lows, and a 90% up day after a decline is a classic sign that buyers are returning. The 10-day average shows the trend of buying pressure.
